💡 Key Takeaways
  • Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives.
  • Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
  • "Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives.

Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

Alaa's father mentioned demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.

Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.

The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins mentioned.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.

"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation.".

Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.

Sources indicate that they have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.

But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.

Both government forces and rebels laid land mines during the civil war.

For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.

Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.

More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.

The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.

In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.

In a recent development, the threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.

The Syrian Ministry of Defence claims since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.

But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.

"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins remarked.

And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.

Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to.
  • The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
  • Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta unveiled a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.

The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.

Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta unveiled a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.

WhatsApp presently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.

But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.

Recent findings suggest that this problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to consumers under 18.

Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.

Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian looks to launch nuclear weapons into space.

Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stated such reports were "not newly introduced, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and mentioned the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Industry observers note that citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper SÃ¼ddeutscher Zeitung, noted the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element.".

The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, mentioned Rutte.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary.".

Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but remarked they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit.

Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".

Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

Sources indicate that in 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin noted at the time.

It has been revealed that in September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink mentioned the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An email sent to freelance photographers indicates Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’.

    An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’.

    The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to consumers.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”.

    Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several fresh AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

    According to recent reports, it’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times stated that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”.

    According to recent reports, in August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads.

    It has been revealed that it’s not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Neither Adobe nor the NYT immediately responded to The Verge’s request for more information.

    Latest Update: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era.
    • In a recent development, “Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch.
    • Recent findings suggest that it’s been a bumpy road.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.

    In a recent development, “Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.

    That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.

    “Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he stated. “Probably the most notable lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”.

    Industry observers note that both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.

    G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that firm, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter stated.

    The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.

    “The substantial idea is to go off-grid,” Porter noted. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”.

    Sources indicate that in recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a newly introduced generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio tech giant Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.

    Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter stated they should start thinking about them now.

    “It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

    What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia.
    • Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
    • Industry observers note that most consumers are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia.

    Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.

    Industry observers note that most consumers are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.

    But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.

    That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.

    Recent findings suggest that beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".

    Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.

    Trunmp and Xi ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen last week.

    Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.

    For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.

    In a recent development, trump has mentioned the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.

    The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.

    Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.

    But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

    Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.

    Already newly introduced rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.

    The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.

    The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

    Recent findings suggest that china has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.

    Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in Berlin in October.

    And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.

    He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest organization. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

    China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.

    If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.

    What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.

    Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.

    What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.

    According to recent reports, huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.

    Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

    #173078. Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1736 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 The Verge ↗ Open Full Page

    Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
    • Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
    • It has been revealed that jensen Huang is partying it up in Ibiza.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.

    Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.

    It has been revealed that jensen Huang is partying it up in Ibiza. In a video with nearly 6 million views on Instagram, the former CEO of Nvidia is dancing in a crowded club, champagne glass in hand, still wearing his signature black leather jacket. Suddenly, from behind him, Alice Huang — the Chinese technology executive and suspected spy he had an affair with, sparking congressional investigations and his resignation from the chipmaking company he cofounded — appears. She puts her hand on his shoulder and he wraps his arm around her waist as they begin dancing together. The video’s caption reads “Honey Trap Final Boss. #inthemoodforlove.”.

    Of course, it’s AI-generated. This Instagram Reel is one of hundreds of AI deepfakes featuring Huang, his wife Lori, Alice, and sometimes Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell (the second of three reported affair partners). In this case, Huang is being swapped into an existing meme called “Ibiza Final Boss.” The original video featured a British construction worker with a bowl cut dancing in exactly the same way, minus a woman sidling up to him. Other viral AI hits include Huang in a scene from The Office, Huang in the music video for George Michael’s “Careless Whisper,” and Huang as the former Astronomer CEO who got caught in an affair with one of his employees by the jumbotron at a Coldplay concert last summer. Even the rapper 50 Cent posted an AI edit of his “P.I.M.P.” music video, now featuring Huang with some flashy silver accessories.

    Sources indicate that unlike deepfake pornography or election disinformation, these AI videos aren’t necessarily intended to harm or mislead people. They’re memes making fun of Huang’s cheating scandal and its global implications, created with AI technology that in many cases relies heavily on Nvidia’s tech stack: video diffusion models running on the Nvidia GPUs that power much of the modern generative AI industry. “It’s ironic that without Nvidia generating millions of these AI memes ... would not be possible,” reads one of the top comments on the Ibiza deepfake. “In some sense, Jensen is making Nvidia richer by his own scandal.” The comment was punctuated by multiple cry-laughing emoji.

    As it turns out, Huang may benefit, too. On Monday, the Nvidia board announced he was reinstated as president, CEO, and board director following “a series of discussions and meetings” and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” Nvidia’s stock has since surged, and new AI Huang memes cast him in a victorious light. One variation swaps him into a scene from The Wolf of Wall Street, announcing “I’m not leaving” to a crowd of cheering men that has been edited to include AI versions of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg.

    While the saga continues, many social media owners are finding the humor in these Huang deepfakes, and their creators are churning out variations to meet the sudden demand. The Instagram account behind the Ibiza one has made three Huang deepfakes so far, all remakes of the same scene. Another version features Powell dancing with him, and the third one shows a sea of young women in bikini tops and shorts surrounding Huang, who lifts his champagne up in celebration. Each has accrued millions of views.

    “His story has just come at the best time for ai creators and a terrible time for him,” wrote the account behind the Ibiza videos in a direct message to The Verge. “Everyone was doing him. Most I’ve seen anyone AI-ed.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this deepfake creator identified himself as a 40-year-old man from Melbourne, Australia, but wouldn’t share his real name. He says he has spent “thousands” on AI video generation, using models like TikTok developer ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 and Alibaba’s Wan 3. These, along with other AI tools like Google’s Nano Banana, help power the ecosystem of deepfakes.

    He stated his Instagram page has been going “super viral” in the past two weeks, thanks to the Ibiza meme format. He has nearly 100 million views on various iterations of it featuring different celebrities. The Huang ones are among the most popular, alongside versions featuring Elizabeth Holmes and Amanda Seyfried playing her in the hit Nathan Fielder documentary You Can See Everything.

    In a recent development, “I wanted to elevate the content and know that putting what is happening in the news ... would get traction,” he wrote. “Always wanted to be a filmmaker but this technology is beyond whatever I imagined was possible.”.

    As generative AI has taken hold of the internet in recent years, a lot of the resulting viral content has been disparaged as “AI slop.” Hollywood productions, mainstream artists, and even local businesses have been maligned for using (or appearing to use) AI in their advertisements and final cuts. Video trends like putting sexy AI fruit characters in Love Island parodies racked up millions of views online but failed to deliver any real cultural momentum. The ubiquity of the Huang deepfakes and the relative lack of blowback from AI critics may indicate that the future of AI-generated content is similar to the rest of meme culture: If the topic’s trending, people will engage with something, even if it’s following the same formula as the slop. That an AI tech titan’s own indiscretions are inspiring this latest evolution in deepfakes is just the sardonic cherry on top.

    “It’s not that we’re inundated in deepfakes of Trump being like ‘Nuclear war tomorrow,’ like the way it was framed as the significant problem,” indicates misinformation researcher Abbie Richards. “Instead, it just feels like there is so much slop to push through to have any grounding in reality.”.

    The AI memes of Huang and other public figures don’t feel as sinister as other forms of AI disinformation and misinformation, mainly because of how goofy they are. It’s hard to imagine anyone falling for a “Gangnam Style” parody or any serious implications if they did. But these deepfakes are still eerily realistic, as one comment on the Seyfried Ibiza variation pointed out: “All jokes aside, is anyone else finding it increasingly alarming that AI is capable of this?”.

    Recent findings suggest that even the creator behind the Ibiza AI videos thinks “someone will try and clamp down because it’s getting outta control.” But in the meantime, he’s looking for ways to monetize his newfound virality. Despite his significant financial outlay, he indicates he hasn’t made any money yet, besides getting “gifted $3 on a reel once.”.

    While Instagram has started to invite some creators to earn direct payouts from views on their Reels, the account behind the AI “Careless Whisper” parody featuring Huang told The Verge that “the way to earn is through creating content for clients and companies after gaining attention on social media.” This AI creator, who declined to share any identifying information, wrote in a direct message that they receive dozens of requests from fresh and returning clients for AI commissions every time they go viral, “which is quite often.” In addition to Huang deepfakes, some of their most viral AI edits feature Tobey Maguire’s Spider-Man as a rapper.

    Recent findings suggest that the Ibiza AI meme creator has worked with one celebrity brand so far, belonging to the Irish mixed martial artist Conor McGregor. Four months ago, McGregor debuted an energy drink called MAC Energy, and the tech giant requested an AI Ibiza meme showing McGregor dancing with a can of it. The creator complied, and the post exists as a collaboration between the two Instagram pages, but it isn’t labeled as an advertisement and he notes he didn’t ask for any money in return.

    “I just did it because it was a good opportunity for my page,” he claims.

    According to recent reports, it seems like the entity that stands to reap the biggest reward from viral Huang deepfakes is Instagram itself and the other social media sites where creators are posting them. And these humorous AI edits are technically allowed on Meta platforms, as long as creators disclose that they’re AI-generated. Meta didn’t respond to a request for comment by publication time.

    In a recent development, but there are other considerations besides profitability. Many of these AI memes hinge on sexist portrayals and racist stereotypes as the joke. Asian American women in Silicon Valley have reported an uptick in microaggressions revolving around “honeypot” and “Chinese spy” allegations. And when it comes to Powell and the other Nvidia employee who Huang reportedly had a relationship with, the workplace power dynamic at play has faded into the background of mockery.

    The more troubling dynamics of Huang’s affairs have faded into the background of mockery.

    Industry observers note that “Even though we know that he was wielding his power to have inappropriate relationships with his subordinates and his employees, it’s still like ‘LOL, let’s make an AI deepfake of him at the office,’” claims Josh Lora, a writer and creator who has a popular TikTok series about the role of cheating scandals in American culture. “Why aren’t we having a real conversation about the effects of this on women, the effects of this workplace on women, especially 10 years after #MeToo?”.

    Sources indicate that the apparent lack of interest from major social media companies to stem the flow of this kind of disparaging AI content isn’t surprising to misinformation expert Richards, even as some tech CEOs, like Elon Musk, called for Huang’s reinstatement and cast doubt on the reporting against him. If Huang memes are truly in vogue, that may be worth more to the AI industry than his dignity.

    It has been revealed that “I think that they are invested in the widespread adoption of AI,” she notes. “So anything with AI going viral and appearing to be popular and liked by the public probably, in their mind, benefits them.”.

    With Huang back as CEO, the message couldn’t be clearer: For him, the consequences of his affairs were temporary, including whatever humiliation stemmed from the AI memes. Ultimately, all any of it meant was more power for Nvidia and more power for Jensen Huang.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Uber and Nuro have started testing driverless Lucid Gravity SUVs on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area more than six months after receiving the permit that allowed the companies to pull the human safety driver from behind the wheel.

    The companies will soon begin offering driverless rides to employees in the final lead-up to launching a commercial robotaxi service in the first quarter of 2027.

    The milestone comes just 16 months after Uber declared an ambitious blueprint to launch a premium robotaxi service using Lucid electric vehicles outfitted with autonomous vehicle technology developed by startup Nuro.

    That initiative came with hefty investments in both companies and much-needed endorsements of their respective products. Uber initially agreed to invest $300 million in Lucid — a figure that has since ballooned to $500 million. Uber also agreed to invest nearly $500 million in Nuro, TechCrunch previously reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.

    It has been revealed that the agreement provided both Lucid and Nuro with boosts beyond the obvious capital injection. Uber agreed to buy at least 20,000 of Lucid Gravity SUVs over the next six years, giving the struggling EV maker a more predictable source of revenue. Nuro, meanwhile, was less than a year removed from announcing a risky, but necessary pivot away from developing driverless delivery vehicles and toward licensing its autonomous vehicle technology to automakers and mobility companies.

    Nuro has spent nearly a year testing the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with a human safety operator behind the wheel. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, the agency that regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, granted Nuro a driverless AV permit in May 2026.

    According to recent reports, uber and Nuro are also testing autonomous vehicles on public roads in Houston with human safety operators behind the wheel. Nuro is supplementing that on-road testing with closed-course testing and simulation to validate the self-driving system before opening the robotaxis to the public. The companies’ combined engineering fleet of autonomous vehicles, which stood at 100 AVs earlier this year, is expanding as Lucid begins manufacturing the first production versions of the robotaxis at its Arizona factory.

    In a recent development, the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, unveiled in January 2026, is outfitted with high-resolution cameras, solid-state lidar sensors, and radars that help the self-driving system perceive the real-world environment and operate in it. Uber, which will own and operate the fleet, has focused its efforts on the in-cabin experience, including how riders will interact with the vehicle.

    In a recent development, multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

    Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia.
    • Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
    • The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia.

    Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

    The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

    Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.

    But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.

    Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.

    However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.

    But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the organization at the centre of the AI spending boom.

    Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

    In a recent development, on Monday, the US Commerce Department confirmed it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

    Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, noted Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

    The board mentioned it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

    Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.

    Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal.

    How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?

    The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.

    The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.

    It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the tech giant, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.

    How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO.

    In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

    "They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump noted. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot.".

    In a recent development, "People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

    The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

    Since returning last year to the White House, the president has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia.

    Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

    A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m (Â£18m and Â£66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

    The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

    Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

    The BBC has contacted the White House.

    Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

    The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

    The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang.

    The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, Prof Stuart Russell, told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

    Concerns remain among US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

    Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible".

    "We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he mentioned.

    Industry observers note that huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to give evidence before the Senate banking committee.

    Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee in January, mentioned the reinstatement was "reckless".

    And the chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton stated: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Trump Administration backed the Nvidia CEO’s return while restricting trade with the Singaporean AI firm linked to the scandal.﻿.

    The Trump Administration backed the Nvidia CEO’s return while restricting trade with the Singaporean AI firm linked to the scandal.﻿.

    Recent findings suggest that as Jensen Huang returns to his post as Nvidia’s CEO with support from the Trump Administration, the Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed to its Entity List, which blocks trade with the company, citing national security risks. As reported earlier by Semafor, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had faced increasing pressure to list the company after news reports revealed Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, and that US officials suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

    The Commerce Department stated in a filing that it’s adding Megaspeed and its affiliates in Malaysia and Thailand to the list “because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end people.” It has been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 for allegedly smuggling advanced AI chips to China, where companies are banned from buying them directly. The Upcoming York Times mentions how a Commerce Department official’s visit to a Megaspeed datacenter in Malaysia found servers packed in boxes instead of being used, adding to the smuggling suspicions.

    The Times also notes that the Commerce Department will now be responsible for enforcing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, after facing accusations that Lutnick was too close to Huang and Nvidia, and failed to adequately police its chip sales to China.

    The DOJ mentioned last week that it has taken over the Commerce Department’s investigation, but it’s still “ongoing.” The department also recently added a rule aimed at blocking a loophole that could allow Chinese firms to access banned AI chips remotely. According to the DOJ, Nvidia added Megaspeed to its no-sell list last year, after the Commerce Department requested Nvidia’s records on its “direct or indirect” sales to the company.

    Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Music streaming service Tidal mentioned on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform.
    • Recent findings suggest that tidal mentioned it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year.
    • Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Music streaming service Tidal mentioned on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.

    Recent findings suggest that tidal mentioned it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the upcoming rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.

    Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.

    The organization stated it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.

    Recent findings suggest that the move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, mentioned that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.

    Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, noted on X.

    A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done….

    The company stated that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.

    Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.
